title: Anointing, Last Supper, Gethsemane, and Arrest
summary: Two days before Passover the chief priests plot Jesus' death, a woman anoints him at Bethany, and Judas agrees to betray him for thirty pieces of silver. Jesus shares the Passover meal with the Twelve, giving them bread and cup as his body and his blood of the covenant, then prays in anguish in Gethsemane while the disciples sleep. He is arrested, abandoned, and tried before Caiaphas and the council, who condemn him for blasphemy, while Peter three times denies knowing him.
story: Jesus has finished his teaching (verse 1 closes the fifth and last of Matthew's great discourses), and the passion begins. Everything he predicted on the road to Jerusalem (16:21, 17:22-23, 20:18-19) now happens in quick succession. The chapter sets devotion beside betrayal and faithfulness beside failure: an unnamed woman honors him while one of the Twelve sells him, and Jesus holds firm in prayer while his closest friends sleep and then run. It ends with Jesus condemned by Israel's highest court and Peter weeping outside. Chapter 27 brings the Roman trial and the cross.
historical:
Passover, the festival remembering Israel's rescue from Egypt (Exodus 12), fell on the fourteenth to fifteenth of the month Nisan in spring and was followed by the week-long Feast of Unleavened Bread. Lambs were sacrificed at the temple in the afternoon and eaten that night in households and groups within the city. Jerusalem's population swelled with pilgrims, and the authorities feared riots, as verse 5 says. Joseph Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long tenure that suggests he worked well with the Roman governors. In 1990 an ornate bone box (ossuary) inscribed with the name Joseph son of Caiaphas was found in a tomb in Jerusalem, and many scholars think it belonged to this high priest or his family.

The Sanhedrin was the council of Jerusalem's leaders, chief priests, elders, and scribes, presided over by the high priest, with authority over Jewish religious and many civil matters under Roman oversight. Later Jewish legal texts forbid capital trials at night or on festival days; scholars debate whether those rules were already in force in the first century, and the Gospels may describe an informal night hearing followed by a formal morning decision (27:1). The broad outline, that Jesus was arrested at the initiative of the temple leadership and handed to the Roman governor, is supported outside the New Testament by the Jewish historian Josephus, writing in the 90s, who says that Pilate condemned Jesus to the cross when he was accused by leading men among the Jews. That passage in his Antiquities was later expanded by Christian copyists, but most scholars think this core statement is his own.
cultural:
Guests at a festive meal reclined on couches around a low table, leaning on the left elbow, and shared dishes by dipping bread into a common bowl. The Passover meal involved unleavened bread, bitter herbs, wine, and the retelling of the exodus, and it closed with the singing of psalms; the hymn of verse 30 was probably from the Hallel (Psalms 113 to 118), traditionally sung at Passover. Many details of the later Passover order are documented only after the temple fell, so how closely Jesus' meal matched them is uncertain.

Perfume like the woman's was a family treasure, often kept in a sealed alabaster flask whose neck was broken to pour it out. Anointing the head honored a guest and was also how kings were marked, while anointing the body belonged to burial. A kiss was the ordinary greeting of a disciple to a teacher, which makes Judas's signal especially painful. Thirty pieces of silver was the compensation the law set for a slave killed by an ox (Exodus 21:32) and the wage paid to the shepherd in Zechariah 11:12, which Matthew will cite in chapter 27. Galileans spoke Aramaic with a recognizable regional accent, which is what gives Peter away.
literary: Matthew builds the chapter from contrasting scenes. The plot of the leaders (verses 3 to 5) and Judas's bargain (14 to 16) frame the woman's generous act (6 to 13). At the supper, the announcement of betrayal is set beside the gift of bread and cup. In Gethsemane Jesus prays three times while the disciples sleep three times, and in the courtyard Peter denies him three times, so that Jesus' threefold faithfulness in prayer and Peter's threefold failure mirror each other. The trial before Caiaphas and the denial in the courtyard happen at the same time, and Matthew cuts between them: Jesus confesses the truth under oath inside while Peter swears falsely outside. Throughout, the language of fulfillment (verses 24, 31, 54, 56) insists that none of this is accident.

outline.t: Passover preparations and the betrayer named
Jesus predicts desertion and Peter's denial
Jesus before Caiaphas and the council

doctrines.note: Jesus interprets his coming death as blood of the covenant poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (verse 28). His death is not a tragic accident but a sacrifice that establishes a covenant and deals with sin, echoing Exodus 24:8 and the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31-34.

The Lord's Supper is instituted here, and Christians have celebrated it ever since. Traditions differ on how Christ is present in it (as a real bodily presence, a spiritual presence, or a memorial), but all see it as Jesus' own gift binding his people to his death and to the coming kingdom.

In Gethsemane Jesus prays honestly for the cup to pass and then submits: not as I will, but as you will. His prayer is the pattern of the Lord's Prayer lived under the greatest pressure, and his warning to watch and pray is addressed to all his followers.

Human plotting, betrayal, and cowardice are real and culpable, yet the Son of Man goes as it is written. God works his purpose through the very acts that oppose it, without excusing those who commit them.

words.note: Diatheke, covenant, the Greek Bible's word for God's binding commitments to his people. At Sinai Moses sprinkled blood and called it the blood of the covenant (Exodus 24:8). Jesus uses the same language of his own blood, presenting his death as the foundation of a renewed relationship between God and his people.

Poterion, cup. At the supper it is the cup of the covenant; in Gethsemane it is the cup Jesus asks to pass from him. In the prophets the cup often stands for God's wrath poured out on sin (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15), which helps explain the depth of Jesus' anguish.

Aparneomai, to deny or disown. It is the word Jesus used when he said his followers must deny themselves (16:24). Peter, who would not deny himself, now denies his Lord. Jesus' prediction and Peter's tears show the word's weight.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as the one who knowingly gives himself up. He predicts his handing over, interprets his death at the supper, accepts the Father's will in Gethsemane, refuses armed defense, and when the high priest demands under oath whether he is the Christ, the Son of God, answers with the affirming “You have said it yourself,” adding that they will see the Son of Man at the right hand of Power, combining Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13. He is also the stricken Shepherd of Zechariah 13:7 whose sheep scatter. The church confesses from this chapter that his death was voluntary and given for many, that he is truly human in his sorrow and truly the Son in his claim, and that he meant his people to remember him at his table until he drinks the cup new in his Father's kingdom.

hard.q: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal, when John's Gospel seems to place the crucifixion on the day the lambs were killed?
hard.a: Matthew, Mark, and Luke clearly present the supper as a Passover meal, eaten on the evening that began the feast, with the crucifixion the next day. John's Gospel places the trial before Pilate on the day of preparation for the Passover (John 19:14), when the priests had not yet eaten it (John 18:28), which seems to put the crucifixion as the lambs were being slaughtered. Several solutions have been proposed. Some think different Jewish groups followed different calendars, so that Jesus kept Passover a day earlier than the temple authorities. Some argue that John's expressions refer to the whole Passover week or to the Friday of Passover week rather than the evening meal itself, which would harmonize the accounts. Others think John arranged his timing theologically to present Jesus as the Passover lamb, or that the Synoptics gave a Passover meaning to a meal eaten the day before. None of these answers has won everyone. All four Gospels agree that Jesus shared a final meal with his disciples at Passover time, was crucified on a Friday, and was raised on the first day of the week.

questions: The woman's gift looked wasteful to the disciples and beautiful to Jesus. What does it look like to give something costly to Christ that others might not understand?
In Gethsemane Jesus is completely honest with the Father about what he wants and completely surrendered to what the Father wills. How does his prayer shape the way you pray in hard seasons?
Peter's failure came right after his loudest promise. What does his story teach about self-confidence, and what hope does it hold for people who have failed?
